## The Foundational Learning Skills module {#c02-fls}

The Foundational Learning Skills (FLS) module was introduced in MICS6 to assess basic reading and numeracy through a household survey.

UNICEF describes the module as assessing skills expected in the early primary grades, with children aged 7–14 as the target population. Because the assessment is administered in households rather than schools, it includes children regardless of whether they are currently enrolled or attending school.

See UNICEF's [Foundational Learning Skills Module](https://data.unicef.org/resources/the-foundational-learning-skills-module/) and the [MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis](https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/MICS6-manual-for-stats-data-analysis-English_2020_v2.pdf).

### What does the module assess?

```text
FOUNDATIONAL LEARNING SKILLS
          │
          ├── READING
          │      ├── oral reading accuracy
          │      ├── literal comprehension
          │      └── inferential comprehension
          │
          └── NUMERACY
                 ├── number reading
                 ├── number discrimination
                 ├── addition
                 └── pattern recognition
```

The released microdata contain substantially more information than a single "meets/does not meet" indicator. Researchers can work with the underlying tasks and items to examine where in the progression children are succeeding or struggling.

::: {.alternativebox-header}
**Do not restrict yourself automatically to the headline indicator**
:::

::: {.alternativebox}
The official binary foundational-skills indicators are useful for reporting a common benchmark, but they discard substantial information. The item-level data allow analysis of individual domains, total scores, patterns of mastery and distributions of performance.
:::

### The assessment is not a conventional school test

The FLS module differs from many international and national learning assessments. It is:

- administered in the child's household;
- administered to a broad age range rather than one school grade;
- able to include children who are out of school;
- relatively short;
- designed around foundational skills expected in early primary school; and
- embedded within a much larger household survey.

This creates research opportunities. Learning can be studied alongside household wealth, family composition, disability, schooling histories and other characteristics collected in MICS.

It also creates comparability issues that researchers need to consider, particularly children's age and grade, whether they are currently in school, the timing of fieldwork within the school year, and the language in which reading was assessed.

Later worked examples show how these features can be incorporated into analysis.

### Official foundational reading skills

UNICEF defines foundational reading skills using three components:

1. oral reading accuracy — the child reads at least 90% of the words in the story correctly;
2. literal comprehension — the child answers all three literal comprehension questions correctly; and
3. inferential comprehension — the child answers both inferential comprehension questions correctly.

A child must satisfy all three to be classified as having foundational reading skills.

This is a demanding conjunctive indicator: failure to meet any one component means the child does not meet the overall benchmark.

The reading assessment is explained in [Understanding the MICS6 reading assessment](#c02-reading).

### Official foundational numeracy skills

UNICEF defines four numeracy tasks:

1. number reading — 6 items;
2. number discrimination — 5 items;
3. addition — 5 items; and
4. pattern recognition and completion — 5 items.

To successfully complete a task, the child must answer all items within that task correctly. To be classified as having foundational numeracy skills, the child must successfully complete all four tasks.

The [UNICEF FLS adaptation guidelines](https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/FL-module-adaptation-guidelines-August-21-2019.pdf) set out these rules in the standard tabulation plan.

The item structure is in [Understanding the MICS6 numeracy assessment](#c02-numeracy).

### FLS and SDG 4.1.1(a)

The MICS6 FLS module was developed to contribute information on foundational reading and numeracy at the Grade 2/3 level. MICS tabulation plans report indicators for children attending Grade 2/3 and for children of the expected age for Grade 2/3, as well as broader age-based tabulations.

When using MICS for cross-country research, distinguish the assessment tasks, the MICS foundational-skills definitions, and the population used for a particular indicator. These are related, but they are not the same thing.
